title: Finite free completed coefficient extension is ordinary derived scalar extension
statement:
Let $\ell$ be a prime, let $E\subset L$ be finite extensions of $\mathbf Q_\ell$ with valuation rings $\mathcal O_E\subset\mathcal O_L$ and uniformizers $t=\varpi_E$, $v=\varpi_L$ [def-weil-l-adic-coefficient-extension], and let $Y$ be any scheme. Work on its small pro-etale site [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site]. Write $R=\widehat{\mathcal O}_{E,Y}=\varprojlim_n(\mathcal O_E/t^n)_Y$ and $S=\widehat{\mathcal O}_{L,Y}=\varprojlim_m(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y$ for the completed coefficient sheaves [def-weil-completed-integral-coefficients], where $(-)_Y$ is the constant sheaf [def-weil-pbc-constant-sheaf]. The inclusions of valuation rings give a canonical map $R\to S$. The $R$-module sheaf $S$ is finite free of rank $[L:E]$.

For $T=R,S$, write $D(T)$ for the derived category of sheaves of $T$-modules [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category, def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Let $K\in D(R)$ be derived $t$-complete [def-weil-derived-complete]. Form ordinary derived change of rings $K\otimes_R^L S$ [lem-pur-derived-change-of-rings]. The reductions $S\to(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y$ induce the canonical completion map
$$
 \chi_{L/E,K}:K\otimes_R^L S\longrightarrow
 R\varprojlim_m\operatorname{Res}^L_m\bigl(K\otimes_R^L(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y\bigr)
 =K\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}\mathcal O_L,
$$
Here $m\geq1$, $\operatorname{Res}^L_m$ is restriction of scalars along $S\to(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y$ [def-pc-sheaf-restrict-scalars], and $R\varprojlim$ denotes the strict-tower cone model specified in [def-weil-integral-scalar-extension], a derived limit [def-weil-derived-limit]. More explicitly, on a K-flat resolution $P\to K$ [def-pc-kflat-complex] the compatible quotient maps $P\otimes_R S\to\operatorname{Res}^L_m(P\otimes_R(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y)$ define a map to the product killed strictly by $1-s$; the induced map to $\operatorname{Cone}(1-s)[-1]$ has zero component in the shifted product. The map $\chi_{L/E,K}$ is the resulting morphism in $D(S)$, independent of the resolution. The last functor is exactly the strict-tower integral scalar extension of [def-weil-integral-scalar-extension], and the right side is interpreted as its derived-limit realization [lem-weil-integral-scalar-extension-well-defined]. This map is an isomorphism, natural in $K$, and $K\otimes_R^L S$ is derived $v$-complete. For $L=E$ it is the natural derived-completeness map $K\to R\varprojlim_n K\otimes_R^L(\mathcal O_E/t^n)_Y$, after the multiplication isomorphism $K\otimes_R^L R\cong K$.

source.place: Lemma 6.8.2(1), pp. 58-59 (completed coefficient sheaves); Definition 3.4.10 and Lemma 3.4.12, pp. 22-23 (completed tensor and derived completeness); Proposition 3.5.1, p. 24 (completion as derived inverse limit). The finite-free coefficient-extension comparison is a consequence of these constructions, not a verbatim numbered lemma. Reduction of completed constant coefficients is Stacks Tag 093M, sites-modules.tex, lemma-completion-flat.

proof.text: By uniqueness of extended absolute values, $\mathcal O_E=E\cap\mathcal O_L$ and $0<|t|_L<1$. The DVR decomposition in $\mathcal O_L$ gives $t=u v^e$ with $u$ a unit and $e\geq1$. Completeness of $E$ implies $\mathcal O_E\cong\varprojlim_n\mathcal O_E/t^n$: choose compatible lifts, whose successive differences lie in $t^n\mathcal O_E$, take their Cauchy limit in $E$, and use the closed unit ball to keep it in $\mathcal O_E$; injectivity follows from $|t|_E^n\to0$. Apply the finiteness-over-complete-ring theorem to $A=\mathcal O_E$, $I=(t)$, $M=\mathcal O_L$. Its separatedness hypothesis follows from $|t|_L<1$. Its finite-quotient hypothesis holds because $\mathcal O_L/t\mathcal O_L=\mathcal O_L/v^e\mathcal O_L$ is a finite set. Thus $\mathcal O_L$ is a finite torsion-free $\mathcal O_E$-module, hence free. Inverting $t$ gives $\mathcal O_L[1/t]=L$ (since $t=u v^e$), so its rank is $d=[L:E]$. Choose a basis $b_1,\ldots,b_d$.

source.place: Tag 031D (lemma-finite-over-complete-ring); DVR finite torsion-free freeness, with the coefficient data as in Bhatt--Scholze 6.8.1

proof.text: For each $n$, the chosen basis and its coordinate inverse give inverse $(\mathcal O_E/t^n)_Y$-module maps $(\mathcal O_E/t^n)_Y^{\oplus d}\leftrightarrows(\mathcal O_L/t^n\mathcal O_L)_Y$, commuting with quotient transitions. The same inverse equations hold after constant sheafification. Ordinary inverse limits may be taken over $m=en$: a compatible family at these indices extends uniquely to index $m$ by reduction from any $en\geq m$, independently of that choice. Taking limits of the basis maps gives $R^{\oplus d}\cong S$, with the prescribed $R$-action, proving finite freeness. Apply the completed-constant-coefficient quotient theorem to $\mathcal O_E,(t)$ and to $\mathcal O_L,(v)$: $R/t^nR\cong(\mathcal O_E/t^n)_Y$ and $S/v^mS\cong(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y$, compatibly with all quotient maps. Its flatness over the discrete constant DVR sheaf also makes multiplication by $t$ on $R$, and by $v$ on $S$, injective: tensor the injective multiplication map of the DVR with its flat completed sheaf. On $S$, $t=u v^e$ is consequently injective too.

source.place: Lemma 6.8.2(1), pp. 58-59; finite-free coefficient argument in the first paragraph of the blueprint scalar-extension composition proof

proof.text:
Choose a K-flat resolution $P\to K$ with flat terms. Ordinary extension is represented by $Q=P\otimes_R S$; change of rings preserves K-flatness and flat terms. For a ring sheaf $T$ and a regular global element $a$, the two-term Koszul complex $[T\xrightarrow{a^n}T]$ in degrees $[-1,0]$ maps quasi-isomorphically to $T/a^nT$ by the quotient in degree zero. Its transition has components $a,1$, so these maps commute with transitions and degree-zero units. Tensoring with a K-flat representative preserves these quasi-isomorphisms. The Koszul reflector therefore identifies the strict derived quotient limit with a locally derived $(a)$-complete object and identifies its canonical unit with the quotient completion unit. Exact countable products represent the derived products; the strict-tower homotopy-limit triangle is computed by the product cone, with the compatible quotient maps giving the zero shifted-product component of the unit. The assumed Roos triangle makes $K$ a derived limit of its quotient tower. Any two such derived limits are isomorphic, so $K$ is locally derived $(t)$-complete because the Koszul reflector's value is. Apply the reflector's unit criterion: the specified quotient unit $\eta_{R,t}:K\to C_{R,t}(K)$ is consequently an isomorphism. This argument uses isomorphism of limit objects only to establish local completeness, never to identify a chosen lift of the reduction map.

The basis in step 2 identifies the underlying $R$-complex of $Q$ with $P^{\oplus d}$, and identifies its $t^n$ quotients and quotient maps with the finite sums of those of $P$. Sectionwise countable products commute with this finite sum, and the cone differential is the corresponding finite block sum. Thus the underlying $R$-map of $\eta_{S,t}:Q\to C_{S,t}(Q)$ is $\eta_{R,t}^{\oplus d}$ and is an isomorphism. Restriction of scalars detects acyclicity: kernels and sheafified cokernels have the same underlying abelian sheaves. Hence $\eta_{S,t}$ is an isomorphism in $D(S)$. Apply the Koszul reflector for $S,t$, whose regularity was checked in step 2; its unit criterion shows that $Q$ is locally derived $(t)$-complete as an $S$-object.

source.place: Lemma 3.4.12, pp. 22-23, and Definition 3.4.10; finite sums applied to the multiplication telescope

proof.text:
The one-generator augmented extended Cech complexes for $S,t$ and $S,v$ are respectively $[S\to S[1/t]]$ and $[S\to S[1/v]]$, in degrees $[0,1]$, with augmentation to $S$ the degree-zero identity. They are canonically identical: $t=u v^e$ gives $1/t=u^{-1}/v^e$ and $1/v=u v^{e-1}/t$, defining inverse localization maps which fix $S$. The extended-Cech completion theorem identifies the derived internal Hom from these augmented complexes as the corresponding reflection units. Since $Q$ is locally $(t)$-complete, its first reflection unit is an isomorphism; the identical augmented complexes give an isomorphism for the $(v)$ reflection unit. Its value is locally $(v)$-complete, so $Q$ itself is locally $(v)$-complete. The Koszul reflector for $S,v$ now gives an isomorphism of its specified quotient completion unit $\eta_v:Q\to C_{S,v}(Q)$, by the regular Koszul-to-quotient comparison in step 3. Its cone triangle and this unit exhibit the Roos completeness condition for $Q$.

Identify that quotient tower termwise: $(P\otimes_R S)\otimes_S S/v^mS\to P\otimes_R(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y$ sends $(p\otimes s)\otimes\bar z$ to $p\otimes\overline{s}z$, with inverse $p\otimes\bar z\mapsto(p\otimes1)\otimes\bar z$. These inverse formulas commute with the differential and quotient transitions and send the map from $Q$ to its original coefficient-reduction map. Therefore the isomorphism of the two product cones carries $\eta_v$ to exactly $\chi_{L/E,K}$, including its zero shifted-product component. The scalar-extension well-definedness theorem identifies this cone with the stated integral functor and its derived-limit realization. This proves all isomorphism and derived $v$-completeness claims.

source.place: Definition 3.4.10, Lemma 3.4.12 and Proposition 3.5.1; the quotient maps identify the strict integral-extension cone

proof.text: For a map of K-flat representatives $f:P\to P'$, each quotient square commutes because both routes send $p\otimes s$ to $f(p)\otimes\overline{s}$. The product squares commute with $1-s$, so the induced cone square gives $\chi_{K'}(f\otimes1)=R\lim_m(f\otimes1)\chi_K$. The derived change-of-rings and integral-extension well-definedness statements, and naturality of the Koszul reflector unit, carry this equality to all morphisms of the derived category. No basis enters the definition of $\chi$. When $L=E$ take the same uniformizer; the inverse multiplication maps $P\otimes_R R\leftrightarrows P$ identify every quotient square with the reduction of $P$. Thus $\chi$ is precisely the canonical completeness unit. For different choices of a uniformizer of the same field the powers define the same ideals and the same quotient maps, giving the same conclusion.
